results.content: ## Effect of Temperature on Rock Fracture ### 5.4.2.3 Characteristics of Crack Branching Crack branching is a common phenomenon in dynamic fracture of some metals [29]. A similar crack branching (or bifurcation) phenomenon was found in dynamic fracture of rocks, too [22,30,31]. When the loading rate was very high, the branching cracks in a specimen went through the specimen, giving rise to three or more fragments, as shown in Fig. 5.6 [22]. Crack branching is one of the main reasons why the dynamic fracture toughness of the rocks increases with increasing loading rates. Crack branching is rarely found on the sections of a specimen fractured under static loading. For example, no branching crack can be found on the sections of specimens C 01 and C 04; see Fig. 4.10. However, one or more branching cracks can be seen on the sections of the specimens fractured under dynamic loading; see Fig. 4.12. : When the loading rate was up to , a different form of branching crack, which usually started from and stopped at the fracture surface, often occurred. : The angle between a branching crack and the fractured surface, which is less than or equal to 90 degree (Fig. 4.12), looks to be increasing with the loading rates [35]. In conclusion, dynamic rock fracture toughness is related to branching cracks. First of all, crack branching within a single element, Fig. 8.19B, requires the design of special elements as described e.g. in Daux et al. results.title: Dynamic tile‐map generation for crack‐free rendering of large‐scale terrain data - Oh - 2025 - ETRI Journal - Wiley Online Library
results.content: # Dynamic tile-map generation for crack-free rendering of large-scale terrain data. While planetary-scale platforms, like Google Earth and Cesium stream data, the streaming of data and the use of regular grid-type digital elevation models lead to cracks among tiles with different levels of detail. They typically employ tile-based rendering with multiple levels of detail (LoD) to manage large-scale data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel dynamic tile-map generation method for crack-free rendering of large-scale terrain data. Section 3 describes the proposed dynamic tile-map generation method to eliminate cracks in streaming- and quadtree-based terrain models. The proposed tile-map generation method efficiently determines the adjacency relationships between terrain tiles rendered in each frame. The primary goal of our tile-map generation method is to identify LoD differences between adjacent terrain tiles, enabling crack-free rendering. In the implemented planetary-scale 3D geospatial application, the LoD difference between the base and neighboring tiles was three levels in max. Intertile cracks in quadtree LoD-based terrain rendering can be minimized by selectively replacing boundary meshes in direct contact with adjacent tiles, according to a precomputed tile map. While this paper focuses on quadtree-based tiles and regular grid DEMs, the core principles of our dynamic tile-map generation method for seamless terrain rendering can be generalized to other spatial data models. To apply our approach, researchers would need to (i) establish a hierarchical spatial indexing scheme (analogous to our quadtree and tile levels) suitable for their chosen data model, along with efficient data organization and retrieval system; (ii) develop techniques for representing and processing multiple LoDs for real-time 3D rendering; and (iii) implement our dynamic tile-map generation method (or an analogous adjacency-based approach) to identify and address potential cracks or discontinuities between spatial units at different LoDs, ensuring a visually seamless terrain model. This paper has presented a novel dynamic tile-map generation method for crack-free rendering of large-scale terrain data in streaming and quadtree-based systems. The proposed method solves significant data processing problems and intertile cracking caused by using multiple LoDs. The implemented platform can render and manage streaming geospatial data in real-time, consisting of approximately 30 TB and 286.3 billion tiles.

results.content: # Add internal boundary or crack in PyGmsh / Gmsh. I am trying to generate a finite element mesh using PyGmsh, using the following code:. mesh = pygmsh.generate_mesh(geom, dim=2). I can generate the following mesh:. However, I would like to add a crack to the mesh, something like:. The crack here is just an example, it would need to be defined before the meshing process. `geom.boolean_difference()` between the final geometry and the line/crack, but this just does not work. The purpose of this type of mesh generation is to simulate a physical crack in a body. In the meshing process, the crack can be modeled by the elemental connectivity of the mesh (i.e. the elements must have different nodes to create a crack face). After applying the load, the crack opens since the element connectivity allows this:. You should do a stress analysis and use post-processing to evaluate the K value for the crack geometry. However, a crack/fracture must be defined. The simplest way is to define it through the element connectivity of the mesh. I think mean just refining the elements along the crack path, but both sides are still joined in the mesh. I would refine the mesh in the area of the crack tip and evaluation the stress intensity factor at integration points as a post processing step. If the crack is not defined like you say, there won't be a concentration of stresses, and it won't be a fracture mechanics problem anymore. Notice that some comercial FEA software already use this technique of modeling the crack through the element connectivity, like Abaqus. I modelled also the crack tip to collapse the nodes in one point by modeling a very small circle. It automatically separates the nodes at the specified crack line/surface. Although it may seem pedantic, a crack should be modelled as a line in a 2D problem (or as a surface in a 3D problem). # "crack" geometry. # embed "crack" on plate. # generate mesh. results.title: David Burch Navigation Blog: Naming and Boundary Conventions on ENC eCharts
results.content: In a recent article (The Strange World of Electronic Chart Boundaries)  I pointed out the unusual nature of the shapes and names of electronic navigation charts (ENC), which are the digitized vector versions of the raster navigation charts (RNC). That is, to make a vector chart of a region, step one is bring out the largest scale RNCs of the region, and then digitize these products in a standard ENC format. Then an echart program can draw the chart on the fly each time we change a display scale or move to a neighboring or overlapping ENC. The primary IHO restriction that affects the boundaries and scales of US ENC is no ENC can overlap an adjacent one within the same scale band. These definitions are useful for selecting charts in catalogs and for understanding the names, and in turn the ENC boundaries we see  in navigation programs. Note too that the US ENC chart numbers are only unique within state designations and scale bands. In learning to use this system we might also keep in mind that the US ENC scale bands are not the same as historically been used in the US for paper charts. The standard US paper chart classifications never had, to my mind, much influence on practical navigation, but the new ENC scale band system does indeed have a meaning, i.e. it determines the third character in the name of any ENC, worldwide. When NOAA sets out to cover the ENC charting of the region covered by 18474 (scale 1:40,000), they start out by digitizing the largest scale RNC charts that cover that region. Note that the Port Orchard and Gig Harbor charts, which are also in scale band 5, are not cut out because they lie wholly within their respective ENC cells. It is not unprecedented that US ENC cover Canadian waters, but in this case we are forced to use the Canadian ENC, because of another IHO requirement that no two Nations can make an ENC of the same waters within the same scale band. This was a direct conflict of overlapping scale bands (note the 4 in each chart name) from two nations, both of which had previous ENC of this region.
